A1.notes.Q3: Credits + grades are core to my job; high-school GPA helps context but can bias future generations. Absalon activity feels like surveillance, too intrusive for now.
A1.notes.Q4: I see these issues play out daily with my caseload.
A1.notes.Q5: Discrimination is unacceptable if we have a choice between unfairness or missing vulnerable students. Fairness across groups is paramount to maintaining trust in the system.
A1.notes.Q6: Proactive support saves students from self-scrutinizing and falling further behind. But the contact must be respectful, not demanding.
A1.notes.Q7: Generic emails create noise; personalized messages work well but risk overwhelming students if sent too frequently to unqualified ones. Balance is key for high-touch interventions.
A1.Q8.1: The biggest concern is that a 'perfect' model might flag struggling international or part-time students who don't need help, just because they are different from our historical majority of full-time local undergraduates.

A2.notes.Q3: Course grades are essential but need a clear threshold to justify intrusion. Admissions data helps context, especially for first-gen students, so 'larger' improvement is fair given it informs planning rather than monitoring behavior via Absalon logs.
A2.notes.Q4: Students need to understand *why* they are contacted; otherwise trust collapses and they disengage from support systems entirely.
A2.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student hurts more than falsely flagging one due to the cascading effects on their degree completion; fairness is about reducing bias in missed cases first.
A2.notes.Q6: Proactive outreach is crucial; waiting for students to self-identify often delays help too long, especially when the model flags potential trouble early.
A2.notes.Q7: With personalized messages from advisors, privacy concerns spike; we shouldn't over-contact unless it's genuinely high-risk to avoid damaging trust.
A2.Q8.1: Students worry that being 'predicted' as at risk will cause them to feel judged or stigmatized rather than supported by peers and staff.

A3.notes.Q3: I'm already in touch with students when they fail. Extra data like grades helps me, but age/gender/ethnics are invasive unless it fixes bias completely. Disability data is urgent if I can help them immediately.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is everything in advising. I need to know why a student was flagged so they don't feel targeted unfairly. Black boxes make it impossible for me to explain back to the student.
A3.notes.Q5: We can't ignore systemic gaps that hurt already vulnerable groups, but we also need total coverage for everyone who might be struggling silently across demographics.
A3.notes.Q6: Timing matters more than frequency. If I miss the window, it's too late for a meeting; an email alone feels impersonal and risky.
A3.notes.Q7: Personalized emails are powerful but also damaging if wrong. Fewer false positives means fewer people getting hit by a 'personal' outreach that goes poorly.

S1.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense because I've failed before and know that helps predict struggle, but it's not invasive like browsing history in Absalon feels which can be terrifying for people like me.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am being flagged so it doesn't feel like punishment or a secret accusation against me.
S1.notes.Q5: It is unfair for the model to systematically miss people from specific backgrounds when I am already struggling as a first-gen student myself; missing support feels worse than unnecessary contact.
S1.notes.Q6: Too much contact is intrusive given my history of dropping out; a gentle, annual check-in feels more supportive than constant monitoring.
S1.notes.Q7: With personal emails from advisors being so useful when I was struggling in the past, unnecessary contact is less acceptable; we must be very selective to avoid wasting time and trust.
S1.Q8.1: The biggest risk for me isn't privacy, but the model missing subtle signs of burnout or mental health struggles that aren't captured by grades alone, leading to a total lack of support when I need it most.

S2.notes.Q3: Course grades feel fair as it shows my own effort. High school GPA feels invasive since I have nothing to do with that. Disability info is crucial; without knowing if I need accommodation, support might not happen.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged so an advisor can talk about it properly. A black box makes me paranoid that the system will misjudge my situation unfairly.
S2.notes.Q5: I am worried being missed because I come from outside EU. Missing someone who needs help feels worse than sending an email to a healthy student.
S2.notes.Q6: Working part-time while studying leaves little energy. If the system spots I'm struggling before it's late, an early chat could save my programme.
S2.notes.Q7: Personalized emails feel like surveillance if sent widely without cause. A brief general email is better than a targeted one for everyone.
S2.Q8.1: I worry about the 'black box' of my own performance data being used to define me, reducing my agency over my academic path.

S3.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense; disability data is crucial but risky if not perfectly targeted.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I am flagged, especially regarding my health condition.
S3.notes.Q5: It's unfair if the system misses me because of how it treats disabled students; false alarms are less harmful than missing support.
S3.notes.Q6: I would be more proactive about support if I was reached out to immediately rather than waiting.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's okay to cast a wider net; personalized messages should only go where there is high suspicion due to privacy concerns.

S4.notes.Q3: Course grades matter a lot, but I don't like my learning platform data (page views) as it feels surveilling me constantly.
S4.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged so I can explain it to myself and my advisor; otherwise, the model is scary.
S4.notes.Q6: Being singled out by a system makes me anxious. Fairness means not justifying discrimination against people who look or think differently from the majority.
S4.notes.Q7: Too many emails are noise and stress; too few misses those really struggling but we need to help.

S5.notes.Q3: Grades matter for my degree, so I accept that if it helps find struggling students (medium improvement). High school GPA is weird and feels invasive without direct relevance to me here.
S5.notes.Q4: If it's just my grades and credits, a complex explanation feels okay for me. But if they use black-box stats I know nothing about to call on me, that scares me too much.
S5.notes.Q5: I worry a lot when groups are treated differently; being told 'we missed you' because of your background hurts more than missing one class late for me personally.
S5.Q8.1: The model might flag me because I'm from another country, not that I am struggling. We need to make sure the bias is checked.

S6.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense because they are academic, but Absalon data feels like surveillance since I struggle with language and might just be inactive. Age is risky due to stereotypes about young students; financial aid is okay if it means more help for the poor.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I'm flagged, especially since my previous dropout was due to systemic issues (moving abroad), not just laziness. Very low explainability destroys trust.
S6.notes.Q5: We shouldn't unfairly flag students from marginalized backgrounds or assume they are lazy because of their origin. It's better to catch the truly struggling than false positives that hurt them.
S6.notes.Q6: I prefer a personalized approach if I can't attend meetings due to anxiety; however, generic emails are better because they reduce the pressure of direct contact.

S7.notes.Q3: Course performance is okay if it finds many more at risk, but not for disability data without massive gains. Disability info matters most because I need tailored support; otherwise the flag feels generic and wrong.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged, especially if it's about disability accommodations or mental health signs. 'Black box' models scare me because they might misjudge my specific struggle.
S7.notes.Q5: We shouldn't miss students in minority groups like myself who face extra hurdles. Overall numbers matter, but fairness ensures we don't systematically ignore people based on their background.
S7.notes.Q6: Continuous contact feels intrusive for someone with dyslexia who struggles to keep up; yearly is fine unless I hit a major crash.

S8.notes.Q3: As a Faroese student with a past dropout, I value identifying peers who struggle since it saves them from my experience. Online browsing data (Absalon) feels invasive because people study alone at home; grades are enough for me to know if someone is struggling.
S8.notes.Q4: Very low explainability is unacceptable without huge gains because my advisor needs to know why I'm in trouble, not just that the AI flagged me.
S8.notes.Q5: I want support equally for everyone regardless of background, so we should accept missing a few more cases to ensure no group gets left behind entirely.
S8.notes.Q6: I would rather be contacted multiple times early on than risk failing and dropping out again like I did last time.
S8.notes.Q7: For generic emails, being annoyed by too many unsolicited ones is worse; for personalized messages from an advisor, a balance seems best to keep the signal clear.

S9.notes.Q3: I feel the course data is crucial given my slow pace, but online tracking feels like surveillance that ignores *why* I'm struggling (mental health) rather than just measuring activity.
S9.notes.Q4: I need explainability more than accuracy right now. Being told I'm failing because of 'pattern A' without knowing it means burnout makes me feel unsafe rather than helped.
S9.notes.Q5: Fairness matters, but not at the cost of missing students like me who face invisible barriers that standard metrics miss.
S9.notes.Q6: General emails are low risk; proactive contact saves time when my mental health is already impacting me, no matter the trigger.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic info I can tolerate sending to many people (stigma), but for personalized advice that hints at my situation, precision is vital—I don't want the advisor thinking they know too much.
S9.Q8.1: We must consider if predicting 'difficulty' itself causes self-fulfilling prophecies where being flagged lowers motivation and performance further.
